techniques.name: DeepLIFT
techniques.description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group training a neural network to predict where a regulatory protein binds DNA computes DeepLIFT scores for each predicted binding region against a reference sequence with background base frequencies. They read off which short stretches of bases carry the score, compare them with known binding motifs, and decide whether the model has learned real regulatory sequence before using it to prioritise experiments.

A hospital imaging team is investigating a chest X-ray classifier that flags healthy patients as abnormal. For the false positives it computes DeepLIFT scores against a blurred copy of each image and checks whether the weight sits on the image border, where scanner labels are printed, rather than on lung tissue. It then decides whether to mask the labels and retrain.

A regional geohazard agency uses a neural network to rate landslide susceptibility from terrain, rainfall and land-cover layers. For a slope the model rates as high risk, DeepLIFT scores show which input layers drove the rating, and the agency compares them with the field investigation report before using the map for planning.

A lender's credit team sends each declined applicant a short statement of the factors that most lowered their score. For its neural network scorer it computes DeepLIFT scores against a documented reference applicant, the median approved applicant, and the statement lists the factors with the largest negative scores, which are the ones that pulled this score below the reference.

limitations.description: Every score is relative to a reference input, and the choice changes the picture. In the original paper an all-zero reference on CIFAR-10 images highlighted hard-to-interpret background pixels, while a blurred copy of the image highlighted object outlines. State the reference used and repeat the analysis with at least one alternative before drawing conclusions.

The Captum implementation supports only the Rescale rule, which can give all the credit to one of two inputs that jointly drive the output. In the paper's min(i1, i2) example Rescale scores only the smaller input, while the RevealCancel rule shares the credit. Where inputs interact, the scores can hide a dependency that a more complete rule would show.

Propagation rules must support the network operations. Captum implements the Rescale rule and a limited set of nonlinearities; inaccessible operations in built-in recurrent modules can prevent attribution unless a supported implementation is used.

Two networks that compute exactly the same function can receive different DeepLIFT scores, because differences between a neuron and its reference do not obey the chain rule that gradients obey (Sundararajan et al., 2017, App. B). The scores therefore describe how the model is built as well as what it computes, which matters when comparing a model with a re-implemented or compressed version of it.

Feature contributions account for a particular output difference, not a causal effect in the world or a guaranteed change after deleting that feature. Correlated genomic bases or financial variables make that distinction important.

resources.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
resources.abstract: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. Video tutorial: http://goo.gl/qKb7pL, ICML slides: bit.ly/deeplifticmlslides, ICML talk: https://vimeo.com/238275076, code: http://goo.gl/RM8jvH.

resources.title: An Attribution Deep Learning Interpretation Model for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly used for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) due to their higher accuracy. However, due to the lack of explanations of the influence of input contributing factors by current DL models, accurately identifying the cause of each landslide remains challenging. This study proposes a novel interpretable DL model named Deep-Attention-LSF, which assigns significance scores to contributing factors at local levels for attributing landslide susceptibility. This model considers the significance scores of input factors to more accurately predict landslide occurrence. DeepLIFT is used as an attribution branching network for interpreting the relationship between input factors and each landslide event. Subsequently, a landslide classification network formed by combining convolutional neural network and long short-term memory is used to predict the landslide occurrence in the entire study area. The performance of Deep-Attention-LSF is tested using the landslide inventory map of Three Gorges reservoir area and the associated maps of 18 landslide-related factors. The accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score of our model were 0.9645, 0.9583, 0.9676, and 0.9522, respectively. These suggest that our model outperformed the compared models, including self-attention LSM, frequency-ratio-attention LSM, bagging and random subspace naive bayes tree, gradient boosting decision tree, random forest, information value model and enhanced C5.0 decision tree model. Deep-Attention-LSF provided reasonable explanations for landslide attributions by comparison with field investigation reports for four specific landslide cases. Combining the interpretation of Deep-Attention-LSF with field investigations can provide more comprehensive information for evaluating specific landslides, providing a useful tool for landslide prevention and management.

techniques.name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
techniques.description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

example_use_cases.description: Identifying which pixels in chest X-rays contribute to pneumonia detection, helping radiologists verify AI diagnoses by highlighting anatomical regions the model considers relevant.

A perception team investigating a misclassified traffic-sign image draws the relevance map for the wrong class. The map shows the relevance sitting on a sticker and the background rather than on the sign itself, which tells the team to add training images with such clutter before the model is retested.

A bank's model-risk reviewers receive LRP relevance scores for a sample of declined applications scored by a neural network. They check that the inputs with the most relevance for the decline output are affordability measures and not proxy fields such as postcode, and file the scores with the decision record for audit.

limitations.description: Each layer type needs its own propagation rule, and a new layer type has none until someone derives one, so adapting LRP to a new architecture takes expertise and testing.
Rule selection (LRP-ε, LRP-γ and others) changes the resulting maps, so two analysts can produce different explanations of the same prediction, and choosing among them takes expertise.

Heatmaps are hard to validate. The original paper judges them by eye and with a pixel-flipping test, and notes that quality beyond visual assessment is an open question, so a plausible-looking map does not prove the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Standard rules do not cover attention layers. Extensions for transformers, such as AttnLRP in the LXT library, exist but are recent and specific to certain architectures, so users of transformers or large language models must adopt them and confirm they match their model.

Bias handling and epsilon stabilisation can absorb or inject relevance, so input scores do not always sum exactly to the selected output. A report should document the accounting residual before claiming conservation.

resources.title: On Pixel-Wise Explanations for Non-Linear Classifier Decisions by Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation
resources.abstract: Understanding and interpreting classification decisions of automated image classification systems is of high value in many applications, as it allows to verify the reasoning of the system and provides additional information to the human expert. Although machine learning methods are solving very successfully a plethora of tasks, they have in most cases the disadvantage of acting as a black box, not providing any information about what made them arrive at a particular decision. This work proposes a general solution to the problem of understanding classification decisions by pixel-wise decomposition of nonlinear classifiers. We introduce a methodology that allows to visualize the contributions of single pixels to predictions for kernel-based classifiers over Bag of Words features and for multilayered neural networks. These pixel contributions can be visualized as heatmaps and are provided to a human expert who can intuitively not only verify the validity of the classification decision, but also focus further analysis on regions of potential interest. We evaluate our method for classifiers trained on PASCAL VOC 2009 images, synthetic image data containing geometric shapes, the MNIST handwritten digits data set and for the pre-trained ImageNet model available as part of the Caffe open source package.

resources.title: Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Explaining Deep Neural Network Decisions in MRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks have led to state-of-the-art results in many medical imaging tasks including Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection based on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. However, the network decisions are often perceived as being highly non-transparent, making it difficult to apply these algorithms in clinical routine. In this study, we propose using layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) to visualize convolutional neural network decisions for AD based on MRI data. Similarly to other visualization methods, LRP produces a heatmap in the input space indicating the importance/relevance of each voxel contributing to the final classification outcome. In contrast to susceptibility maps produced by guided backpropagation ("Which change in voxels would change the outcome most?"), the LRP method is able to directly highlight positive contributions to the network classification in the input space. In particular, we show that (1) the LRP method is very specific for individuals ("Why does this person have AD?") with high inter-patient variability, (2) there is very little relevance for AD in healthy controls and (3) areas that exhibit a lot of relevance correlate well with what is known from literature. To quantify the latter, we compute size-corrected metrics of the summed relevance per brain area, e.g., relevance density or relevance gain. Although these metrics produce very individual "fingerprints" of relevance patterns for AD patients, a lot of importance is put on areas in the temporal lobe including the hippocampus. After discussing several limitations such as sensitivity toward the underlying model and computation parameters, we conclude that LRP might have a high potential to assist clinicians in explaining neural network decisions for diagnosing AD (and potentially other diseases) based on structural MRI data.

sample_claims.text: On the audited sample of chest X-rays, the relevance for the pneumonia output lies mainly inside the lung fields and not on laterality markers, text or image borders.
For every audited credit decision, the relevance scores for the decline output are stored with the decision record, and they sum to the model's score within the stated tolerance.
In the reviewed true positives of the defect-detection network, most of the relevance falls on the defect itself and not on the background texture that differs between production lines.

Where the perception model misclassifies a traffic sign in the test set, the relevance map shows whether the evidence for the wrong class came from the sign or from its surroundings, and each case is recorded.

techniques.name: Contextual Decomposition
techniques.description: Contextual Decomposition explains why an LSTM, a neural network that reads text one word at a time, made a particular prediction. The user picks a word or phrase, and the method splits the network's output score into two parts: the part due to that phrase alone, and the part due to everything else, including how the phrase interacts with the words around it. Comparing a phrase's score with the scores of its parts reveals effects that word-by-word methods miss, such as a negation reversing the sentiment of the word that follows it. The split is tracked through the LSTM's internal gates, so the model itself is not changed or retrained. The output is a numerical score for each phrase examined.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing why an LSTM-based spam filter flagged an email by decomposing contributions from individual words ('free', 'urgent') versus their contextual interactions ('free trial' together).

A hospital analytics team checks an LSTM that flags clinical notes mentioning possible pneumonia. Contextual decomposition shows whether negated findings such as 'no evidence of pneumonia' push the score down, as intended, or whether the model reacts to the word 'pneumonia' alone, which tells the team if it needs retraining on negated examples before use.

A platform's trust-and-safety team handles an appeal against an LSTM toxicity classifier's removal of a post. The reviewing moderator is shown the phrases with the highest contextual decomposition scores, including whether a negation such as 'not stupid' was read correctly, so the moderator can judge whether the removal rested on the post's actual meaning.

limitations.description: Developed for LSTMs, whose gates the method uses to separate a phrase's own effect from its interactions. The source does not cover plain recurrent networks, transformers or attention models, so teams using those cannot apply the published method as it stands.
Needs internal states, gate parameters and classifier weights. Output labels or probabilities alone do not reveal the phrase-related and remaining-input components.

The user must choose each phrase to examine, and the published method handles contiguous phrases. The number of possible phrases grows quickly with text length, so scanning a whole document for interactions is costly and easy to leave incomplete.

The split relies on linearising the gate and activation functions and averaging over orderings of the terms. Interaction scores are therefore approximate, and the source validates them only on sentiment tasks (Stanford Sentiment Treebank, Yelp), so scores on other tasks need checking independently.

Components combine additively in hidden states and class scores before the probability transformation. They should not be read as independent probabilities or as the exact effect of deleting a phrase.

resources.title: Beyond Word Importance: Contextual Decomposition to Extract Interactions from LSTMs
resources.abstract: The driving force behind the recent success of LSTMs has been their ability to learn complex and non-linear relationships. Consequently, our inability to describe these relationships has led to LSTMs being characterized as black boxes. To this end, we introduce contextual decomposition (CD), an interpretation algorithm for analysing individual predictions made by standard LSTMs, without any changes to the underlying model. By decomposing the output of a LSTM, CD captures the contributions of combinations of words or variables to the final prediction of an LSTM. On the task of sentiment analysis with the Yelp and SST data sets, we show that CD is able to reliably identify words and phrases of contrasting sentiment, and how they are combined to yield the LSTM's final prediction. Using the phrase-level labels in SST, we also demonstrate that CD is able to successfully extract positive and negative negations from an LSTM, something which has not previously been done.

resources.title: Interpreting patient-Specific risk prediction using contextual decomposition of BiLSTMs: Application to children with asthma
resources.abstract: Background Predictive modeling with longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data offers great promise for accelerating personalized medicine and better informs clinical decision-making. Recently, deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance for many healthcare prediction tasks. However, deep models lack interpretability, which is integral to successful decision-making and can lead to better patient care. In this paper, we build upon the contextual decomposition (CD) method, an algorithm for producing importance scores from long short-term memory networks (LSTMs). We extend the method to bidirectional LSTMs (BiLSTMs) and use it in the context of predicting future clinical outcomes using patients’ EHR historical visits. Methods We use a real EHR dataset comprising 11071 patients, to evaluate and compare CD interpretations from LSTM and BiLSTM models. First, we train LSTM and BiLSTM models for the task of predicting which pre-school children with respiratory system-related complications will have asthma at school-age. After that, we conduct quantitative and qualitative analysis to evaluate the CD interpretations produced by the contextual decomposition of the trained models. In addition, we develop an interactive visualization to demonstrate the utility of CD scores in explaining predicted outcomes. Results Our experimental evaluation demonstrate that whenever a clear visit-level pattern exists, the models learn that pattern and the contextual decomposition can appropriately attribute the prediction to the correct pattern. In addition, the results confirm that the CD scores agree to a large extent with the importance scores generated using logistic regression coefficients. Our main insight was that rather than interpreting the attribution of individual visits to the predicted outcome, we could instead attribute a model’s prediction to a group of visits. Conclusion We presented a quantitative and qualitative evidence that CD interpretations can explain patient-specific predictions using CD attributions of individual visits or a group of visits.

sample_claims.text: In the clinical-note classifier, negated findings such as 'no evidence of pneumonia' lower the score for that condition, as the contextual decomposition of the full phrase shows.
Each removal decision of the toxicity classifier that is sent to appeal can be traced to named words or phrases whose contextual decomposition scores account for most of the output score.

In the news-sentiment model used for credit monitoring, the contribution of a sentiment word changes sign when a negation or contrast precedes it, and contextual decomposition separates the word's own effect from its context.

For the audited support tickets, the routing model's decision is not driven by any single trigger word: phrase-level contextual decomposition scores account for more of the output than the strongest single-word score.

techniques.name: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
techniques.description: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) explains individual predictions by approximating the complex model's behaviour in a small neighbourhood around a specific instance. It works by creating perturbed versions of the input (e.g., removing words from text, changing pixel values in images, or varying feature values), obtaining the model's predictions for these variations, and training a simple interpretable model (typically linear regression) weighted by proximity to the original instance. The coefficients of this local surrogate model reveal which features most influenced the specific prediction.

example_use_cases.description: Explaining why a specific patient received a high-risk diagnosis by showing which symptoms (fever, blood pressure, age) contributed most to the prediction, helping doctors validate the AI's reasoning.
Debugging a text classifier's misclassification of a movie review by highlighting which words (e.g., sarcastic phrases) confused the model, enabling targeted model improvements.

Showing insurance customers the claim features that most influenced an automated approval or denial. A reviewer first checks that the explanation is stable across repeated runs and plausible for that claim, because it approximates the model locally and may not match its full reasoning.

limitations.description: Explanations can be unstable due to random sampling, producing different results across multiple runs.
The linear surrogate may poorly approximate highly non-linear model behaviour in the local region.
Defining the neighbourhood size and perturbation strategy requires careful tuning for each data type.
Can be computationally expensive for explaining many instances due to repeated model queries.

Assumes features are independent when generating perturbations, producing unrealistic out-of-distribution samples for datasets with correlated features. This can generate misleading attribution scores when inputs share strong correlations (e.g., age and income in credit scoring, comorbidities in clinical data).

resources.title: "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
resources.abstract: Despite widespread adoption, machine learning models remain mostly black boxes. Understanding the reasons behind predictions is, however, quite important in assessing trust, which is fundamental if one plans to take action based on a prediction, or when choosing whether to deploy a new model. Such understanding also provides insights into the model, which can be used to transform an untrustworthy model or prediction into a trustworthy one. In this work, we propose LIME, a novel explanation technique that explains the predictions of any classifier in an interpretable and faithful manner, by learning an interpretable model locally around the prediction. We also propose a method to explain models by presenting representative individual predictions and their explanations in a non-redundant way, framing the task as a submodular optimization problem. We demonstrate the flexibility of these methods by explaining different models for text (e.g. random forests) and image classification (e.g. neural networks). We show the utility of explanations via novel experiments, both simulated and with human subjects, on various scenarios that require trust: deciding if one should trust a prediction, choosing between models, improving an untrustworthy classifier, and identifying why a classifier should not be trusted.

resources.title: Lime — basic usage, two class case (lime project tutorial)
Evaluating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations on Clinical Machine Learning Classification Models
resources.abstract: The usage of black-box classification models within the healthcare field is highly dependent on being interpretable by the receiver. Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanation (LIME) provides a patient-specific explanation for a given classification, thus enhancing the possibility for any complex classifier to serve as a safety aid within a clinical setting. However, research on if the explanation provided by LIME is relevant to clinicians is limited and there is no current framework for how an evaluation of LIME is to be performed. To evaluate the clinical relevance of the explanations provided by LIME, this study has investigated how physician's independent explanations for classified observations compare with explanations provided by LIME. Additionally, the clinical relevance and the experienced reliance on the explanations provided by LIME have been evaluated by field experts. The results indicate that the explanation provided by LIME is clinically relevant and has a very high concordance with the explanations provided by physicians. Furthermore, trust and reliance on LIME are fairly high amongst clinicians. The study proposes a framework for further research within the area.

Explanations of the same prediction, repeated with fresh random samples, name the same top features, so the stated reasons do not depend on chance.

The content moderation system provides interpretable explanations for individual moderation decisions without requiring access to model internals

techniques.name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
techniques.description: A ridge regression surrogate approximates a complex model with a linear equation fitted to the complex model's own predictions. The complex model is run on a set of inputs, and ridge regression, a linear model with a penalty that keeps coefficients stable when features are correlated, is fitted to reproduce its outputs. Each coefficient then shows roughly how far a feature moves the complex model's output, averaged over those inputs. Fidelity, often reported as R-squared (the share of the model's variation the surrogate reproduces on held-out inputs), shows how far the coefficients can be trusted. They describe the complex model, not the real world.

example_use_cases.description: A model-risk team at a bank fits a ridge surrogate to a gradient-boosted credit-scoring model's scores on a held-out sample, reports how closely the surrogate reproduces them, and uses the standardised coefficients to brief the model-risk committee on which inputs drive scores overall.

A hospital analytics team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural network that predicts readmission risk from tabular records, to check that the features driving the network's predictions overall, such as age and prior admissions, are plausible to clinicians. The findings concern the network, not what causes readmission.

An energy company's forecasting team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural-network load forecaster using a year of hourly weather and calendar inputs, and reads the standardised coefficients to confirm that temperature and time of day dominate. A low R-squared during heatwaves leads the team to record that the surrogate does not describe the model in that regime.

An insurer's compliance team gives a regulator a ridge surrogate of its pricing model together with held-out R-squared and a table of each feature's contribution to a sample of quotes, so the regulator can check the stated drivers against the model's actual outputs.

limitations.description: A linear surrogate cannot represent interactions or thresholds. Where the complex model relies on them, the surrogate fits its predictions poorly and its coefficients describe a different model. Report held-out R-squared and treat a low value as a failed surrogate.

A good average fit can hide poor fit in parts of the input space, such as rare groups or extreme values, so the coefficients may be wrong for exactly the cases that matter. Check fidelity within subgroups and near decision boundaries.
There is no agreed fidelity level above which a surrogate can be trusted. Whether 50%, 80% or 99% of variance explained is enough depends on the use, so the reviewer has to set and justify a cut-off.

Ridge shrinks every coefficient and shares weight between correlated features. Coefficient sizes depend on the penalty strength and on feature scaling, so compare them only after standardising the features, and report the penalty used.

The surrogate explains the complex model's behaviour on the sampled inputs, not the real-world link between features and outcomes. Reading its coefficients as causes, or as evidence about the data, will mislead.

resources.title: Extracting Tree-Structured Representations of Trained Networks
resources.abstract: A  significant  limitation  of  neural  networks  is  that  the  represen(cid:173) tations  they  learn  are  usually  incomprehensible  to  humans.  We  present a  novel algorithm , TREPAN,  for extracting comprehensible,  symbolic representations from  trained neural  networks.  Our algo(cid:173) rithm uses  queries to induce a  decision tree that approximates the  concept  represented by  a  given  network.  Our experiments demon(cid:173) strate that TREPAN is  able to produce decision trees that maintain  a high level of fidelity to their respective networks while being com(cid:173) prehensible  and  accurate.  Unlike  previous  work  in  this  area,  our  algorithm is  general in its applicability and scales well  to large net(cid:173) works  and problems with  high-dimensional input spaces.

sample_claims.text: A ridge surrogate reproduces the credit model's scores on held-out applications with an R-squared of at least 0.9, and its five largest standardised coefficients identify the inputs that drive scores overall.
The surrogate of the readmission-risk model reproduces the model's predictions closely within every age band tested, so its coefficients describe the model's behaviour for each of those bands.

The demand-forecasting model depends mainly on temperature and time of day overall, as shown by a linear surrogate whose fit to the model has been measured, with the lower fit during heatwaves reported as a limit.
Where the linear surrogate's fit to the model falls below the stated threshold, the model is recorded as not summarised by a linear surrogate, and no coefficient is cited as an explanation of it.

The regulator holds the pricing model's ridge surrogate with its held-out R-squared and a table of each feature's contribution to a sample of quotes, and can check the stated drivers against the model's outputs.

techniques.name: ANCHOR
techniques.description: ANCHOR explains one prediction of a black-box classifier with an if-then rule, called an anchor, such as 'age > 30 AND income < £50k'. An anchor names a small set of feature conditions under which the model keeps giving the same prediction, whatever the other features are. To find one, the method fixes the conditions, varies the other features by sampling, asks the model for a prediction each time, and searches for the broadest rule that holds in at least a chosen share of the samples, commonly 95%. Each anchor comes with its estimated precision and its coverage, the share of cases to which it applies. Both figures describe the model's behaviour on the sampled variations, not on real cases, and continuous features are first grouped into ranges.

example_use_cases.description: A model-validation team at a lender computes anchors for a sample of declined applications from a gradient-boosted credit model. It checks that the conditions holding each decision, such as a low credit-score band together with recent missed payments, match credit policy, and reads each rule's coverage to see how many other applications it applies to.

A hospital data team explains individual alerts from a tabular sepsis-risk model with anchors, and a clinician checks whether the conditions in each rule, such as raised temperature and white-cell count, are clinically sensible or point to an artefact such as the ward an admission came from.

An employer's compliance team gives a reviewer the anchor behind a shortlisting prediction, with its precision and coverage. The reviewer tests the rule on other applications and can challenge it if it leans on an attribute that should not matter, such as age.

limitations.description: The stated precision is measured on perturbed samples from a chosen sampling distribution, not on real cases. If that distribution produces unrealistic inputs, or is skewed by an unbalanced training set, the figure can overstate how far the rule can be relied on.

An anchor covers only the inputs its conditions match, often a small share. In the original experiments average coverage ranged from about 1% to 29% on tabular data, so one anchor says little about the model as a whole. Choosing a set of anchors helps but adds effort.

Predictions close to the model's decision boundary, or of rare classes, need long, very specific rules with little coverage, which add little insight. Strict precision thresholds make this more likely.

Continuous features must be grouped into ranges before rules can be stated, and the grouping changes which anchors are found. Too coarse hides boundaries, and too fine gives narrow rules with little coverage.

Each anchor needs many queries to the model, so run time depends on how fast the model is and on the number of features. The method is built for classifiers, so a numeric output must first be turned into classes.

resources.title: Anchors: High-Precision Model-Agnostic Explanations
resources.abstract: We introduce a novel model-agnostic system that explains the behavior of complex models with high-precision rules called anchors, representing local, "sufficient" conditions for predictions. We propose an algorithm to efficiently compute these explanations for any black-box model with high-probability guarantees. We demonstrate the flexibility of anchors by explaining a myriad of different models for different domains and tasks. In a user study, we show that anchors enable users to predict how a model would behave on unseen instances with less effort and higher precision, as compared to existing linear explanations or no explanations.

resources.title: Interpretability in HealthCare A Comparative Study of Local Machine Learning Interpretability Techniques
resources.abstract: Although complex machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, Neural Networks) are commonly outperforming the traditional simple interpretable models (e.g., Linear Regression, Decision Tree), in the healthcare domain, clinicians find it hard to understand and trust these complex models due to the lack of intuition and explanation of their predictions. With the new General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the importance for plausibility and verifiability of the predictions made by machine learning models has become essential. To tackle this challenge, recently, several machine learning interpretability techniques have been developed and introduced. In general, the main aim of these interpretability techniques is to shed light and provide insights into the predictions process of the machine learning models and explain how the model predictions have resulted. However, in practice, assessing the quality of the explanations provided by the various interpretability techniques is still questionable. In this paper, we present a comprehensive experimental evaluation of three recent and popular local model agnostic interpretability techniques, namely, LIME, SHAP and Anchors on different types of real-world healthcare data. Our experimental evaluation covers different aspects for its comparison including identity, stability, separability, similarity, execution time and bias detection. The results of our experiments show that LIME achieves the lowest performance for the identity metric and the highest performance for the separability metric across all datasets included in this study. On average, SHAP has the smallest average time to output explanation across all datasets included in this study. For detecting the bias, SHAP enables the participants to better detect the bias.

sample_claims.text: For a sample of declined loan applications, each decision of the credit model is held in place by a short rule over policy-relevant features, with estimated precision of at least 95% under the stated sampling distribution.

Sepsis alerts raised by the risk model are each explained by a rule over clinical measurements, and a clinician reviewed a sample of rules and found none that relies on an administrative field such as ward or admission time.
The set of rules chosen to explain the classifier covers at least half of the validation cases, so the main patterns it relies on have been examined.
Each shortlisting decision from the screening model can be given to a reviewer as a rule with its precision and coverage, so that the reviewer can test the rule on other applications.
Every reason given for an individual model output states its own coverage, so a reviewer knows which other cases the reason applies to and which it does not.

techniques.name: Concept Activation Vectors
techniques.description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

example_use_cases.description: Auditing a medical imaging model to check whether its chest X-ray classifications are sensitive to diagnostic concepts (like 'tumour characteristics') or to irrelevant ones (like 'scanner type' or 'patient positioning'), so the clinical team can judge whether the model relies on medically relevant information.

A team auditing an image classifier used for content tagging builds concept sets from photographs of people of different ethnicities and genders, with random photographs as the comparison, and tests each output class for significant sensitivity to those concepts, as the original paper did. Classes with significant sensitivity to an ethnicity or gender concept are listed for retraining with balanced data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A developer of a driver-assistance system documents, for a type-approval authority, how its traffic-sign classifier responds to visual concepts. The report gives significance-tested TCAV scores for the 'stop sign' class against concepts such as graffiti, snow cover and low sun glare, so the authority can see what the classifier's predictions are sensitive to.

limitations.description: Requires clearly defined concept examples and non-concept examples, which can be hard to obtain for abstract or subjective concepts. If the examples differ from the random counter-examples in other ways, such as image source or lighting, the CAV mixes those differences in with the concept.

Assumes the concept is represented as a direction that a linear classifier can pick out at the chosen layer. If the concept is not linearly separable there, the CAV is unreliable, so check that the classifier separates the two sets well before reading any scores.

Results depend heavily on which layer is examined, because layers capture different levels of abstraction. A concept can be invisible at one layer and strong at another, so a single-layer result should not be generalised.

The significance test trains hundreds of classifiers per concept and layer (the paper uses about 500), so cost multiplies with the number of concepts and layers tested. FastCAV, a 2025 preprint, reports speed-ups of up to 63.6 times.

Scores are class-level and describe sensitivity, not cause. A TCAV score is the share of a class's inputs whose score rises along the concept direction, so it does not explain an individual decision, and a high score does not show that the concept causes the prediction.

resources.title: FastCAV: Efficient Computation of Concept Activation Vectors for Explaining Deep Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Concepts such as objects, patterns, and shapes are how humans understand the world. Building on this intuition, concept-based explainability methods aim to study representations learned by deep neural networks in relation to human-understandable concepts. Here, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) are an important tool and can identify whether a model learned a concept or not. However, the computational cost and time requirements of existing CAV computation pose a significant challenge, particularly in large-scale, high-dimensional architectures. To address this limitation, we introduce FastCAV, a novel approach that accelerates the extraction of CAVs by up to 63.6x (on average 46.4x). We provide a theoretical foundation for our approach and give concrete assumptions under which it is equivalent to established SVM-based methods. Our empirical results demonstrate that CAVs calculated with FastCAV maintain similar performance while being more efficient and stable. In downstream applications, i.e., concept-based explanation methods, we show that FastCAV can act as a replacement leading to equivalent insights. Hence, our approach enables previously infeasible investigations of deep models, which we demonstrate by tracking the evolution of concepts during model training.

resources.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
resources.abstract: The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size, complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net’s internal state in terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important to a classification result–for example, how sensitive a prediction of “zebra” is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a medical application.

resources.title: Global and Local Interpretability for Cardiac MRI Classification
resources.abstract: Deep learning methods for classifying medical images have demonstrated impressive accuracy in a wide range of tasks but often these models are hard to interpret, limiting their applicability in clinical practice. In this work we introduce a convolutional neural network model for identifying disease in temporal sequences of cardiac MR segmentations which is interpretable in terms of clinically familiar measurements. The model is based around a variational autoencoder, reducing the input into a low-dimensional latent space in which classification occurs. We then use the recently developed `concept activation vector' technique to associate concepts which are diagnostically meaningful (eg. clinical biomarkers such as `low left-ventricular ejection fraction') to certain vectors in the latent space. These concepts are then qualitatively inspected by observing the change in the image domain resulting from interpolations in the latent space in the direction of these vectors. As a result, when the model classifies images it is also capable of providing naturally interpretable concepts relevant to that classification and demonstrating the meaning of those concepts in the image domain. Our approach is demonstrated on the UK Biobank cardiac MRI dataset where we detect the presence of coronary artery disease.

resources.title: Concept attribution: Explaining CNN decisions to physicians
resources.abstract: Deep learning explainability is often reached by gradient-based approaches that attribute the network output to perturbations of the input pixels. However, the relevance of input pixels may be difficult to relate to relevant image features in some applications, e.g. diagnostic measures in medical imaging. The framework described in this paper shifts the attribution focus from pixel values to user-defined concepts. By checking if certain diagnostic measures are present in the learned representations, experts can explain and entrust the network output. Being post-hoc, our method does not alter the network training and can be easily plugged into the latest state-of-the-art convolutional networks. This paper presents the main components of the framework for attribution to concepts, in addition to the introduction of a spatial pooling operation on top of the feature maps to obtain a solid interpretability analysis. Furthermore, regularized regression is analyzed as a solution to the regression overfitting in high-dimensionality latent spaces. The versatility of the proposed approach is shown by experiments on two medical applications, namely histopathology and retinopathy, and on one non-medical task, the task of handwritten digit classification. The obtained explanations are in line with clinicians' guidelines and complementary to widely used visualization tools such as saliency maps.

sample_claims.text: The chest X-ray classifier's 'pneumonia' predictions are significantly sensitive to clinically recognised findings and not significantly sensitive to scanner type or patient positioning, at the layers tested.

The content-tagging classifier's TCAV scores for the ethnicity and gender concept sets are recorded for every output class at the tested layers, and the classes with significant sensitivity are listed for review.
The traffic-sign classifier's sensitivity to graffiti, snow cover and glare concepts is documented with significance-tested TCAV scores for each sign class the approval authority has requested.
The object recogniser's class predictions depend mainly on concepts that domain experts regard as meaningful for that class, such as shape and texture, rather than on background concepts.

techniques.name: Forward Simulation Test
techniques.description: A forward simulation test checks whether people who have studied a model's explanations can predict the model's output for inputs they have not seen, so it tests with people the understanding an explanation method is assumed to give, where fidelity checks only compare the explanation with the model by computation. Doshi-Velez and Kim proposed it as a human-grounded evaluation of interpretability: participants are given an explanation and an input and must state what the model will output, whether or not that output is correct. In the controlled design of Hase and Bansal, participants study a set of examples with the model's outputs, predict the outputs for a separate set of test inputs, then study the same examples with explanations added and predict the same test inputs again, and the gain in accuracy is credited to the explanations (a separate group that studies the examples without explanations guards against a practice gain); the test inputs are kept apart from the explained examples so that explanations cannot give the answers away, and are chosen so that the model is right and wrong equally often, so that predicting the true label scores no better than chance. A counterfactual variant, in Hase and Bansal's form, shows an input, the model's output and its explanation, and asks what the model will output for an edited version of that input, with edits chosen so that half change the output. The result is the change in the share of correct predictions, with a confidence interval, for each explanation method or design compared; it is evidence that people can anticipate the model on the kind of input tested, not that they make better decisions with it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team must choose between feature-attribution bar charts and a short rule list as the explanation shown to credit analysts for a loan-default model. It runs a forward simulation test with 30 credit analysts on past applications, balanced between correct and incorrect model predictions, and adopts the rule list only if its gain over the no-explanation baseline is clearly larger than that of the bar charts; otherwise it treats the two as equal.

An online platform's trust and safety team uses the counterfactual variant to test whether moderators who see which words a toxicity classifier weighted can predict whether it will still flag a comment after one of those words is replaced. A score no better than the baseline tells the team that the highlights do not show how the classifier responds to edits, before it writes moderation guidance that relies on them.

A research team choosing between counterfactual images and saliency heatmaps for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier shows each group of participants explained example images, then asks them to predict the classifier's decision on 12 other images, three from each cell of its confusion matrix, without explanations. It takes forward to a study with clinicians the explanation whose group predicts best, measured against a group that saw the examples without explanations.

A local authority plans to show caseworkers, who are outside the team that built it, the reasons behind a housing-benefit fraud-risk score. Before releasing the reasons in that form, it runs a forward simulation test with caseworkers on unseen cases, half of them cases the score got wrong, using the reasons exactly as they will appear, and revises them if caseworkers who studied them predict the flag no better than caseworkers who did not.

limitations.description: A pass shows that people can anticipate the model, not that they decide better with it. Buçinca et al. found that results on a task of predicting an AI's decisions did not predict results on the real decision task, and Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al. found that people who could better simulate a simple, clear model did not follow it more when that helped, and in some experiments were less able to correct its large mistakes. A claim about decisions needs a decision study.

The test is easily made trivial. If the explained examples are reused as test items, explanations that show the predicted class or a probability give the answer away, and if the model is mostly right, participants can score well by predicting the true label. Hase and Bansal found earlier studies that reused the same items for explanation and prediction; results from such designs overstate what the explanation conveys.

Effects are often small against the variation between people and items. With 32 trained undergraduates and about 180 to 320 responses per condition, Hase and Bansal's 95% confidence intervals on the change in accuracy were about 8 to 13 percentage points either side, and only LIME on tabular data clearly improved both forward and counterfactual simulation. A study must be sized for the difference it needs to detect, with a bootstrap over both participants and items.

The score holds for the people tested. Many studies use students or crowd workers because domain experts are costly to recruit, which Doshi-Velez and Kim give as the reason this kind of evaluation is cheaper; a result from lay participants does not show that the clinicians, analysts or caseworkers who will use the explanation can predict the model.

The before-and-after design credits any gain to the explanations, but participants see the same examples and test items twice, and Hase and Bansal had no group that repeated both phases without explanations, so a practice gain is not ruled out. Their participants also found it hard to remember the explained examples while predicting, so the number of examples and the time allowed must be fixed and reported when methods are compared.

resources.title: Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
resources.abstract: As machine learning systems become ubiquitous, there has been a surge of interest in interpretable machine learning: systems that provide explanation for their outputs. These explanations are often used to qualitatively assess other criteria such as safety or non-discrimination. However, despite the interest in interpretability, there is very little consensus on what interpretable machine learning is and how it should be measured. In this position paper, we first define interpretability and describe when interpretability is needed (and when it is not). Next, we suggest a taxonomy for rigorous evaluation and expose open questions towards a more rigorous science of interpretable machine learning.

sample_claims.text: Credit analysts who studied the rule-list explanations predicted the loan-default model's output on unseen applications more accurately than at their no-explanation baseline, on a test set balanced between correct and incorrect model predictions.

Caseworkers who studied the fraud-risk reasons predicted the score's flag on unseen cases, half of them cases the score got wrong, more accurately than caseworkers who studied the same cases without the reasons, and above the accuracy threshold set in the evaluation plan.

Moderators shown the toxicity classifier's word weightings predicted whether an edited comment would still be flagged more accurately than before they saw the weightings, on a set of edits half of which changed the classifier's decision.

Participants who studied the counterfactual images predicted the pneumonia classifier's decisions on separate, unexplained images more accurately than participants who studied the saliency heatmaps, on a test set in which the classifier was wrong as often as it was right.
